The area does have an interesting local commercial center, probably once quite vital, and though now somewhat under-realized, nonetheless still functioning. The railroad bridge over-passing Delmas Avenue, with its consequent change in street grade, represents a highly coherent transition/entrance between the two principal districts of Gardner.
Finally, a fourth visually distinct district occurs in the extreme southwestern corner of the project area. This sub-area is not defined by strong boundaries, but rather it is the uniformity of the environment which distinguishes it. If ever there were an example of how an organized street tree plan can unify an area, this district should be it. The streets are lined soley by Sycamores planted at regular intervals; the well-maintained residences, usually in the bungalow style, are of uniform height, mass, setback. And with all these unifying elements, the street pattern shifts at an angle to assure variety and visual interest to the perspective. This fourth district is certainly a high-quality work of urban residential design.
Mayfair CNRA:
The primary development of Mayfair occurred more recently than did that of the other project areas, mainly taking place within the last twenty-five years. Because of its later development, the area's street pattern is more influenced by the automobile. Whereas the regularity of the grid makes the streets of the older neighborhoods all more or less equal, in Mayfair there is a hierarchy to the street pattern. The basic unit is the "superblock," defined by major arterials such as Alum Rock Avenue, San Antonio Street, Kammerer Avenue, Sunset Avenue, and Jackson Avenue. Within the "Superblock", large tracts of houses are constructed; the single tract of 40 or more lots is equivalent to the single lot along the grid of the campus area, or the 3-5 adjacent lots containing the same bungalowstyle house in Olinder or Gardner. In effect, by 1950 urban development patterns had increased in scale in response to the automobile. Ideally, the "superblock" is designed to step down in scale. The arterial street, such as Alum Rock Avenue, includes the commercial stores and shopping centers designed to attract the motorist passing by at relatively high speed (store design, basically horizontal, often has an eye-catching vertical mass functioning as a signpost, and always generous parking lots are provided to transition the shopper from the street to the store entrance). In contrast, the "superblock's" collector and residential streets work at a more intimate scale, appropriate to their residential use.
However, the ideal "superblock" pattern is only partially fulfilled in Mayfair. Firstly, the wide sweep of Highway 680 and the meandering course of Silver Creek break up the continuity of the arterial and collector streets. Secondly, the development of tracts within the block's boundaries was only partially achieved.
Approximately one-third of the area was constructed in tract houses (usually duplexes), laid out by civil engineers to achieve the greatest usable land area with a minimum of street frontage, and designed by architects to offer perhaps 3-4 different floor plans.
